chapter.title: Outline of a document

abstract.para: &suse; documentation is modular. Articles bundle topics, which are small information units with one purpose each, into documents. Books are comprehensive guides to a subject area of a product, such as system administration. This chapter describes the topic types, the structure of articles and books and the rules for abstracts, metadata and revision histories.

revdescription.para: Restructured the Outline chapter: added modular documents, topic types and the structure of articles, and moved the structure of books to a separate section

chapter.para: A topic is a small information unit with one purpose. A topic works on its own, so several documents can reuse it. &suse; publishes two forms of documents: articles and books.

Articles are the standard form. An article is an assembly of topics that serves one distinct purpose. Books are comprehensive guides that consist of chapters and, in larger books, parts. Maintain existing books in the structure that is described in . Write new content as articles.

sect1.title: Modular documentation
sect1.para: This section describes the principles of modularity, the topic types and the structure of an article. For the detailed information about working with modular documentation, including effective abstracts, ITS tags and revision history, see .

sect2.title: What is modular documentation?
sect2.para: The goal of modular documentation is to produce sets of adaptable, solution-based, easy-to-find and reusable documents. Rather than covering a complete technology or a set of problems, each article serves one distinct purpose and stands for itself. It includes the requirements, context, instructions, troubleshooting and frequently asked questions that readers need for that purpose.
Apply the following principles when you write topics:

listitem.para: Write each topic for one purpose. If a topic serves two purposes, split it into two topics.
Write each topic so that it stands alone. Include the context that readers need in the topic itself.
Write each topic so that other articles can reuse it. Do not refer to other topics by position, for example, in the previous section.
Put the most important information first. Lead each section with a direct answer or summary.
Use the same term for the same thing in all topics. For more information, see .

sect2.para: Bundle topics into an article with an assembly file. An assembly file is an organizational unit that structures the topics into a coherent and meaningful document. It contains the metadata of the article and references the topics in the order in which they appear. Find the templates for assemblies and topics in the doc-modular repository.

sect2.title: Topic types
sect2.para: Use one of the four topic types in for every topic.

row.entry: Instructs readers how to perform a task
Noun phrase, such as CLI interface
Provides basic facts such as settings, options and parameters
Noun phrase, such as Configuration options
Helps readers navigate and links to related information
Fixed name, such as For more information

sect2.para: Use the same title pattern for all topics at the same level. For more information, see . The following rules apply to the topic types:

listitem.para: A task topic describes how to reach one goal. State the goal first. Then list preconditions or prerequisites and describe the actions in a procedure.
A concept topic explains what something is and why it matters to the reader. Do not describe steps in a concept topic. Use paragraphs and, where they help, lists and figures.
A reference topic provides facts that readers look up, such as settings, options and parameters. Use tables or variable lists. For more information, see and .
A glue topic helps readers navigate and combines texts or structures that fit no other type. Typical glue topics are For more information and What's next. See more details in .

sect2.title: Structure of an article
sect2.para: For articles, use a document structure that includes the following elements, in that order:

listitem.para: title and (optional) subtitle
metadata
revision history
abstract
(optional) prerequisites
topics, structured as sections and subsections
(optional) troubleshooting
(optional) more information
(optional) glossary
(optional) appendixes

formalpara.title: Title and subtitle
formalpara.para: Use title-style capitalization for the title. Do not add a product version number to the title. The subtitle is optional. For more information, see .

formalpara.title: Metadata
formalpara.para: Provide a meta title, a meta description and a social description in the designated meta elements of the assembly. For more information, see and .

formalpara.title: Revision history
formalpara.para: Add a revision history and update it for significant changes. List the newest entry first. For more information, see .

formalpara.title: Abstract
formalpara.para: Summarize the topic of the article in 40–80 words. For more information, see . For more information, see .

formalpara.title: Prerequisites
formalpara.para: Use a short itemized list directly after the abstract to name what readers need before they start, such as required access or permissions. Omit the element if readers need nothing.

formalpara.title: Topics
formalpara.para: Create a topic for every major task, concept or set of reference facts. Structure the topics as sections and subsections. Start every section with an introductory paragraph. For more information, see and .

formalpara.title: Troubleshooting
formalpara.para: Collect common mistakes and problems in a section named Troubleshooting. Always use this name. Mark up the problems with the qandaset element. To describe solutions to more than ten problems, add topical subsections with qandadiv elements below the Troubleshooting section.

formalpara.title: For more information
formalpara.para: Collect Web links to all sources of information that are helpful in a given context in a glue topic named For more information. Follow the general referencing guidelines in and when you create such sections.

formalpara.title: Glossary
formalpara.para: A glossary contains important terms in alphabetical order and provides a brief explanation for each. Add a glossary if the article uses terms that are new to the target audience. For more information, see .

formalpara.title: Appendixes
formalpara.para: Place appendixes after the glossary. Use them for supplementary material that does not fit into a topic.

formalpara.title: Contributors
formalpara.para: Writing documentation is a collaborative effort. Credit the contributors on the title page if five or fewer contributors, all from outside the documentation team, create and maintain the content. This rule applies to articles and small documents, such as &suse; Best Practices.

sect2.para: The table of contents is generated automatically.

sect1.title: Books
sect1.para: A book is a comprehensive guide to a subject area of a product, such as system administration. It consists of chapters and, in larger books, parts that group related chapters. This section describes the structure and the elements of a book.

sect2.title: Structure of a book
sect2.para: For books, use a document structure that includes the following elements, in that order:

listitem.para: a preface
chapters, split into sections
(optional) a glossary
(optional) appendixes

sect2.para: For books with many chapters, create parts at the outline level above chapters.

sect2.title: Title page and imprint
sect2.para: Both the title page and the imprint are created automatically, but depend on information being present in the book. Provide the following information:

formalpara.title: Title
formalpara.para: Work with the product manager to define the book title. Do not use the product name and version in the book title.

formalpara.title: Product name and product version
formalpara.para: Work with the product manager to find the correct product name and version number. Mark up this information with productname and productnumber, respectively.

formalpara.title: Documentation version or revision information
formalpara.para: Optionally, use the releaseinfo element to mark up version or revision numbers of the documentation itself.

formalpara.title: Revision history
formalpara.para: Every book, part and chapter that is included in a build must contain a revision history. For more information, see .

formalpara.title: Copyright notice
formalpara.para: Use the standard copyright notice reproduced in . Change the starting year of the copyright protection to the current year.

example.title: Standard copyright notice
example.screen: <legalnotice> <para> Copyright © [starting year]–<?dbtimestamp format="Y"?> SUSE LLC and contributors. All rights reserved. </para> <para> Permission is granted to copy, distribute and/or modify this document under the terms of the GNU Free Documentation License, Version 1.2 or (at your option) version 1.3; with the Invariant Section being this copyright notice and license. A copy of the license version 1.2 is included in the section entitled <quote>GNU Free Documentation License</quote>. </para> <para> For &suse; trademarks, see <link xlink:href="https://www.suse.com/company/legal/"/>. All other third-party trademarks are the property of their respective owners. Trademark symbols (®, ™ etc.) denote trademarks of &suse; and its affiliates. Asterisks (*) denote third-party trademarks. </para> <para> All information found in this book has been compiled with utmost attention to detail. However, this does not guarantee complete accuracy. Neither SUSE LLC, its affiliates, the authors nor the translators shall be held liable for possible errors or the consequences thereof. </para> </legalnotice>

sect2.title: Elements of a book
sect2.para: Besides the title page and the imprint, a book contains the following elements:

listitem.para: Use an abstract to summarize the information provided in a book, chapter or set in 40–80 words. For more information, see .
The table of contents is generated automatically.
Include a brief overview of the content of a manual, related manuals and typographical conventions. The preface can also contain information about its target audience.
If you are writing a book with many chapters, create parts at the outline level above chapters. Make sure that each part contains at least three chapters. Keep part titles clear and concise.
Do not use product version numbers in chapter titles. They affect the output of data analytics.
Chapters typically consist of the following elements. Appendixes are an exception.

formalpara.title: Abstract
formalpara.para: In an abstract, summarize the topic instead of summarizing the outline. For more information, see .

formalpara.title: Introduction
formalpara.para: Provide introductory information directly after the abstract. Do not place it in a separate section.

formalpara.title: Sections
formalpara.para: Structure the detailed information, so readers can skim the text. Create sections for every major task, such as installing, configuring, monitoring and administering. If helpful, split sections into subsections. Avoid nesting deeper than three levels of sections.

listitem.para: Start sections with an introductory paragraph outlining the focus of the section. If the section describes a sequential task, add a procedure description. Steps of a procedure can contain a cross-reference to subsections where topical background is provided and an action is explained in detail.

formalpara.title: Troubleshooting
formalpara.para: Collect common mistakes and problems in a section named Troubleshooting. Always use this name. Use the qandaset element to mark up the problems. To describe solutions to more than ten problems, add topical subsections with qandadiv elements below the Troubleshooting section.

formalpara.title: For more information
formalpara.para: In a section named For more information, collect Web links to all sources of information that are helpful in a given context. Follow the general referencing guidelines in when you create such sections.

listitem.para: The optional glossary contains important terms in alphabetical order and provides a brief explanation for each. For more information on creating lists of terms, see .

Writing documentation is a collaborative effort. To give credit to all contributors, add an appendix to the book that points to the Contributors page of the respective GitHub repository. For an example, see .
The preceding rules are a minimum. In addition, make sure that the contributors appendix is compliant with the document license.
